title: Managing Services with systemd
intro: On nearly every modern Linux server, long-running services are managed by systemd. Knowing its handful of core commands is non-negotiable for operations work.

steps.prompt: List all running services on this machine.
steps.fake_output:
UNIT              LOAD   ACTIVE SUB     DESCRIPTION
nginx.service     loaded active running A high performance web server
api.service       loaded active running API Server
sshd.service      loaded active running OpenSSH server daemon
steps.explanation: Every service systemd knows about, with its current state.
steps.why: This is your inventory of what's actually running — useful on an unfamiliar server before touching anything.

steps.prompt: Check the detailed status of the nginx service.
steps.fake_output:
● nginx.service - A high performance web server
   Loaded: loaded (/lib/systemd/system/nginx.service; enabled)
   Active: active (running) since Sat 2026-09-27 08:00:12; 2h ago
 Main PID: 812 (nginx)
steps.explanation: Two different things matter here: 'active (running)' is the current state, 'enabled' means it will start on boot.
steps.why: A service can be running right now but DISABLED, meaning it will silently not come back after the next reboot — exactly the trap in linux-incident-001. Always check both words.

steps.prompt: You just edited nginx's config. Reload it without dropping active connections.
steps.explanation: reload tells the service to re-read its config without a full stop/start, if the service supports it.
steps.why: 'restart' kills and restarts the process, dropping every in-flight request. For services that support it (nginx does), 'reload' is the zero-downtime option. Run 'nginx -t' first to validate the config — a broken config plus restart takes the site down.

steps.prompt: You just created a new unit file at /etc/systemd/system/worker.service. Make systemd pick it up.
steps.explanation: systemd caches unit files; daemon-reload re-reads them from disk.
steps.why: Forgetting daemon-reload after creating or editing a unit file is one of the most common systemd mistakes — your changes simply don't exist yet as far as systemd is concerned, and start/restart uses the stale version.

steps.prompt: Start the worker service AND enable it to start on boot, in one command.
steps.explanation: --now combines enable (start on boot) with start (start right now).
steps.why: Running only 'start' leaves you with a service that works until the next reboot and then mysteriously vanishes. 'enable --now' is the one-shot way to make it both running and persistent.

steps.prompt: Follow the worker service's logs live.
steps.fake_output:
Sep 27 10:15:02 worker[9021]: Connected to queue
Sep 27 10:15:03 worker[9021]: Processing job 1
(streaming...)
steps.explanation: -u filters to one unit, -f follows new lines as they arrive.
steps.why: Same idea as tail -f or kubectl logs -f, but for anything systemd manages. Add --since '10 min ago' to see recent history before following.
